title: Bandsmen's resentment and the huddles that scattered when he approached
summary: Randolph felt resented by some of the men, though not only New Orleans musicians, who would break up their huddles when he walked over.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: How did you feel about that? You're the -- I know on records you're the only trumpet player -- or one of the few trumpet players who soloed on a Louie Armstrong record.
Yes, that's right. Well, but you know what -- the boys, you know, one don't know how you feel when guys look -- like resent you, you know. Why would they do that?
There were a lot of New Orleans musicians in that band. Was that part of that New Orleans thing? You know how clanish the New Orleans musicians are.
I don't know. It could have been -- no, but some of the boys was from here, though -- some of them was from here.

And, as a matter of fact, the boys would be out talking in a huddle, you know -- you know how the musicians stand out talking, and I'm straightening up the music on the rack or doing something then I'd go out and say, "Well, fellows, hi, fellows," and everybody would scatter.
